I slammed my hands on the metal table, getting right in his face. "What kind of hallucinogenic gas did you pump into those vents? How the hell do you make three hundred sane people butcher each other in one night while you just sit there and watch?!"

Lucian slowly raised his eyes. They were completely empty—like looking down a bottomless well. No malice, no sadistic joy. Just a freezing void. He smiled genuinely and spoke with a voice as soft as velvet.

"Drugs are a cheap parlor trick for the weak, sir. I didn’t use anything physical. We just had a chat. Five minutes of conversation with every doctor and guard. That’s all it took to bring the house down."

I scoffed, feeling the heat of anger in my chest. "Bullshit. You can’t talk a normal person into a massacre just by shooting the breeze, no matter how slick you think you are."

He tilted his head slightly, talking to me as if explaining basic math to a toddler.

"Humans are incredibly fragile machines, Elaric. You don’t need to push them off the cliff. You just have to politely convince them that falling is the only way to fly. Every human hides a secret shame, a buried grudge, or a crippling inferiority complex. I just find that tiny, rusted screw in their heads... and I give it a quarter-millimeter turn. I hand them the moral high ground to do what they secretly wanted to do all along. After that? The machine just eats itself alive begging for salvation."

My jaw clenched. "You’re a sick psycho. But right now, you’re chained to a desk in a black site. You ain't God. You’re a ghost we bagged, and I’m gonna put a needle in your arm myself."

Lucian’s smile widened. For the first time, it looked like genuine pity.

"Did you really bag me? Let’s trace the invisible threads, Director Elaric. Twelve years ago, you were a nobody detective about to get the boot. Then, boom—an anonymous leak exposed your boss's corruption, sliding you right into his chair. Four years ago, the only politician threatening to gut your department? Found hanging from his ceiling fan. Last year, the cartel boss who put a hit on your little girl? Sold out by his right-hand man and caught a bullet to the dome. You really think that was just dumb luck? Cosmic justice?"

My lungs stopped working. Ice water dripped down my spine. Only I knew those details.

Lucian leaned in, the heavy chains rattling against the table.

"Who do you think mailed those files? Who do you think whispered in that politician’s ear that a scandal would ruin his daughters forever, and that a noose was the most honorable, heroic way out? Who do you think bought that cartel underboss a cheap beer and convinced him he was born to wear the crown?"

He looked dead into my soul.

"I don’t have an army. I don’t have cash. I don't even have a name for your little folders. I never show my face. But I engineered your entire reality. You’re sitting on that high horse thinking you have free will, thinking you're a self-made legend... but you're just a pet project I threw together. I built you from scratch, step by step, just to see if I could craft a 'mythical hero'. And now... I wanted a front-row seat to see how that hero breaks when he realizes he’s nothing but a wooden puppet, and I hold the strings."

I lost it. I unholster my Glock and shoved the barrel right between his eyes. My hand was shaking like a leaf. "You're full of shit! I built my own life! I’ll blow your sick brains out right now and end this!"

He didn’t blink. He just looked at the barrel of my gun with profound tenderness.

"You can pull the trigger. But before you do... ask yourself: Why haven't the two armed guards outside that door checked the viewing window for the last half hour? And why has your wife's phone been going straight to voicemail since this morning?"

I swallowed hard. It tasted like razor blades.

"I had a very brief chat with your guards before you walked in. One is drowning in gambling debt, the other just found out his kid has leukemia. I promised them the one thing you can't give them: absolute chaos. As for your wife... I bumped into her at the grocery store yesterday. Crying in the aisle, per usual. She told me she feels like a burden, that her depression is dragging you down. I didn't disagree. I just validated her feelings... and explained, with pure, gentle logic, how swallowing that entire bottle of sleeping pills would be the ultimate act of true love."

The gun slipped from my fingers, hitting the concrete floor with a deafening clatter. I collapsed to my knees, gasping for air, frantically fumbling for my phone to call her, but my hands were entirely paralyzed by dread.

As I broke down on the floor, Lucian stood up slowly. The heavy iron cuffs slid right off his wrists—he had quietly dislocated his own thumbs at the start of the interrogation without flinching or showing a single drop of pain.

He walked to the heavy steel door and opened it. My two elite guards were standing right there. Tears were streaming down their faces, but their rifles were aimed directly at my chest, ready to shred me to pieces just to please his invisible will.

Lucian looked back at me one last time, his empty eyes swallowing the dim light of the room.

"I'm not a monster, Elaric. I'm just a mirror reflecting the absolute ugliest parts of your souls. And now... the mirror is leaving to build another world."

The pale kid walked out into the dark hallway, fading like a ghost that never existed. He left me trapped on the floor, crying in the burning hell of my own life, finally realizing that me, and everyone in this city, were nothing but numbers in a math equation solved by a monster with a gentle smile.

I’m not usually one to post on these sites, but I need your help.

I just celebrated my 36th wedding anniversary with my husband, Terry.

Terry took me out to eat at Ruby’s where we’d had our first date. We ate steaks, had wine, and even made love.

Everything was going great.

Except one thing.

Terry died about three days ago.

Now, I realize you may be confused at this point. I certainly was at first. He did die. I’m sure of it, because I found him. Terry has always been a deep sleeper. He even had a CPAP machine for the last five years or so because he slept so deeply he stopped breathing. He had obstructive sleep apnea where his airway was restricted when he laid down.

Today was like any other day at first.

Since it was our anniversary, I got up quietly, made coffee, and started to get ready for work with the bathroom door closed. Terry usually slept late on Wednesdays so I didn’t think anything odd when he didn’t move as I got up.

It wasn’t until I got out of the shower and went back through the bedroom that things started to feel weird. Terry usually would take his mask off and lay in bed for a few minutes while I showered and when I came out of the shower, I’d make sure he got up. It was our little routine.

Except that morning, when I said “Happy anniversary, sweetheart. I made some coffee,” he didn’t move.

His CPAP was still on and he looked kind of funny.

It was eerily quiet.

The CPAP machine usually made this constant low roaring sound when it forced air through the tubing and into his mask so Terry could breath. I’d gotten so used to it I hardly even heard it anymore.

I heard its absence though.

It was dead silent.

I had one towel wrapped around my head and another around my body. Both my hands were occupied with keeping those in place so I bumped his foot with my bare leg, but he was ice cold.

And stiff.

“Terry, babe, are you ok?”

But, he wasn’t.

I had to pry that mask off his face and lift him up in the bed to check his heart and his lungs.

No heartbeat. No breath.

His eyes were closed, thank god, but he’d already started to turn a funny shade of bluish purple. It was a disturbing sight. His face was the worst of it. Along his cheek red marks lined where his mask had been like he’d tried to claw it off, but couldn’t.

I was so shocked I couldn’t even scream.

I didn’t call anyone.

I didn’t even move for what felt like hours, but must have only been a few minutes.

My hair was still wet.

I don’t even remember crying.

That’s the weird thing.

Like I could almost tell myself it didn’t even happen.

Especially after what happened later.

I know this is the part where you’re going to judge me. But it is what it is.

I left him there in the bed and went to work.

I didn’t know what to do.

It’s not like I could deadlift him by myself.

I wrapped him in the covers he was laying on and shut the bedroom door.

Then I drove to work.

I must have been in shock.

When I got there, Melanie’s car was already there along with some other part time staff. A few of them were standing by the door since they didn’t have a key to get in.

I parked and let them in the library and headed to circulation where my office is.

When I turned the corner, Melanie stood frozen in the lobby like she’d seen a ghost. She was facing towards the mirrored stairway at the center of the building. She had such a funny look on her face, now that I think about it.

When she saw me, she snapped back to her usual smile and waved to me. I waved back. Then I watched her walk back up the stairs.

I looked back at the mirror again after she’d left. I had crossed the lobby and walked over near the stairs where the main light switches were.

I saw how tired I looked in the image reflected back at me. I hadn’t realized how dark the material was before. It had a smoky beauty I’d never noticed.

Something pulled me closer.

I noticed motion behind me.

In the mirror.

At first I thought it was just the part-timers coming in for the day, but I turned around and nobody was there.

Voices carried out from the break room in the distance.

I turned back around.

There, right behind me, was Terry.

I’m not sure if I was scared or relieved.

I just stared at him.

I didn’t bother to look back.

I knew he wouldn’t be there.

What I did instead was even more surprising to me.

I reached out my hand and touched the mirror.

My fingers brushed against the cool obsidian surface and for a moment nothing happened.

Then I felt it.

Something was pressing back from the other side.

Soft at first then with more and more pressure.

Finger tips came first.

Then a hand.

An arm.

A shoulder.

Then a head.

Terry’s head.

Followed by the rest of him.

I backed away and couldn’t help but stare, open-mouthed.

He smiled. My Terry’s smile. The one he’d given me the first time we’d met.

In this very room.

Tanya came around the corner and waved at the both of us.

“Hey, Dusty!”

“Aw, that’s sweet that Terry came with you today! Happy Anniversary, guys!”

“Great to see you, Terry! How’s the tomato crop this year?”

Terry smiled.

His usual smile.

Then he waved.

Tanya waved back and moved off around the desk.

He didn’t move his mouth or his body.

I grabbed Terry’s hand and walked us out to the parking lot and we both got into my car and drove away.

I called my boss from the car saying that I was sick so I wouldn’t have to go back to work.

When we got home, the other Terry was still there. Wrapped in those sheets. Except something was wrong. The smell was unbearable. Like rotten meat. I asked Terry to help me put the other Terry in the closet so he wouldn't stink up the house.

For some reason, Terry wasn’t speaking still. But he had the same kind eyes. And his smile.

I realize you may judge me for doing what I did and not getting help or telling anyone outside of this forum.

I don’t expect you to understand.

Terry is all I have.

We got dressed that night and celebrated our anniversary like we planned.

I had my Terry back.

It was a miracle.

That was three days ago.

I haven’t been back to work.

I read on the news about what happened to Bobbie. They said he dug out his eyeballs and carved the words ARE YOU SCARED into his chest by the time they found him. He’d crawled into an air duct on the third floor of the library. He’d been muttering something about mirrors, apparently. He had been admitted to the state mental hospital for observation. The news had a field day with the coverage.

I had a couple missed calls from friends and colleagues from work. One from an unknown number. Management had contacted the police.

There was some kind of investigation.

Jesus, I don’t know what to do.

I can’t bring myself to open the closet.

I can’t lose Terry again.

I won’t.

But I think something is wrong with him. The one that came back.

I told him to stay in the guest room until we can figure out what to do.

He won’t or can’t speak.

Sometimes, he gets angry like he doesn’t know where he is.

He’s been banging on the wall since the sun went down a couple hours ago.

BANG.

BANG.

BANG.

I don’t know what to do. I’m scared if I talk to the police, they’ll take Terry away.

I’m just afraid he may not have been the only thing that came back through that mirror.

My daughter died five years ago. Even now, half a decade later, typing those words out feels fundamentally wrong. She was only nine years old when a sudden, aggressive illness took her. It was three agonizing days in a hospital room filled with the steady beep of heart monitors, and then, just like that, she was gone. There are some types of pain that never actually leave your body; you just eventually learn how to carry the weight so it doesn't crush you completely. For five years, my nightly routine has been exactly the same: I look at her photograph on the mantel piece before bed, and I wish for the one impossible thing every grieving parent wants. Just one more conversation. One more hug. One more chance to tell her I love her.

Last night, I got my wish. And I will regret it for the rest of my life.

At exactly 2:17 AM, I was startled awake by three soft, rhythmic knocks on my front door. I know the precise time because I immediately checked my phone, assuming it was a neighbor or a late-night delivery mistake. But when the knocking came a second time, a strange, suffocating silence seemed to fall over the house. I got out of bed, crept into the living room, and looked through the peephole. My knees instantly gave out, and I nearly collapsed onto the floorboards.

My daughter was standing on the concrete porch outside. She was barefoot, her hair was tangled, and she was wearing the exact same pink pajamas she had been buried in. Her face was completely soaked with fresh tears.

"Daddy," she whispered through the wood.

My hands shook so violently I could barely turn the deadbolt. Every rational thought, every law of science and nature completely vanished from my mind. I threw the door open and she lunged forward, throwing her small arms around my neck. She felt entirely real. She was warm, solid, and smelled faintly of the strawberry shampoo she used to love. I held her so tightly against my chest I thought I might break her, sobbing uncontrollably into her hair while she wept into my shoulder. For a few beautiful, delusional minutes, the last five years of grief were completely erased.

Then, the cracks started to show.

I pulled back slightly to look at her, but she wouldn't meet my eyes. Every time I tried to look directly at her face, her gaze would frantically twitch away, staring at the floor, the walls, anywhere but at me. I asked her where she had been, how she was here, if the hospital had made a mistake—but she remained completely silent, just clutching the fabric of my shirt with a white-knuckled grip.

Finally, she leaned up and whispered directly into my ear: "Don't let it know I'm here."

A cold, sickening dread spread through my stomach. "What? Bug, what are you talking about?"

She slowly turned her head toward the dark hallway leading to the back of the apartment, her crying shifting into a terrified hyperventilation. "It followed me."

I immediately looked down the hall, shifting her behind me. There was nothing there. Just the familiar, empty shadows of my home. But when I turned back to comfort her, her face was twisted in absolute horror. She wasn't looking at the front door anymore. She was staring right past my shoulder, looking at the empty space directly behind me.

"Daddy..." her voice cracked, turning into a breathless whimper. "It's smiling."

I spun around so fast I nearly tripped. The hallway was still completely empty. But the air had instantly changed. The darkness down the corridor seemed deeper, heavier, as if the hallway itself had stretched out and grown longer than it was supposed to be. My daughter started backing away from me toward the open front door, her eyes still locked on the empty shadows behind my back.

Before I could reach out to grab her hand, she said something that froze the blood in my veins: "It wore my face first."

Instantly, the power cut out. Every single light in the house died at the exact same second, plunging the room into pitch-blackness. I heard my daughter let out a sharp, piercing scream. I lunged blindly toward the sound, my hands clawing through the empty air, finding nothing but cold space.

Then came the footsteps. It wasn't just one person running. It was the sound of dozens of bare feet, slapping frantically against the hardwood, circling around me in the dark. They were moving impossibly fast, coming from every single corner of the room at once, closing in on me. Right alongside the footsteps, a horrific wave of static odors hit my nose—the smell of wet, freshly dug earth, mixed with sharp hospital disinfectant and the sickeningly sweet scent of rotting funeral flowers.

In a panic, I fumbled with my phone and snapped the flashlight on. The bright beam cut through the living room.

The heavy darkness vanished. The footsteps stopped. The apartment lights flickered back to life, humming softly. My daughter was gone.

I spent the next three hours frantically searching every square inch of the house. I checked every closet, under every bed, inside the kitchen cabinets, screaming her name until my throat was raw. Nothing. But when I finally walked into the bathroom, I saw them.

Muddy footprints. Small, child-sized tracks made of wet, dark earth. They started at the bathroom tile, led directly up to the sink, and walked straight toward the mirror. But they didn't stop in front of the glass. The final pair of muddy prints stopped inside the reflection, as if whoever made them had simply walked directly through the glass and into the wall.

I didn't go back to sleep. I sat on the living room couch with every light turned on, clutching a baseball bat, waiting for the sun to rise. Around 6:00 AM, just as the first gray light of dawn started filtering through the windows, my phone buzzed in my hand.

It was a push notification from an old baby monitor app. It’s an app I haven't used or opened in half a decade—the account was disabled, and the physical camera that used to sit in my daughter's bedroom was thrown into a dumpster years ago. Her old room is completely empty now, used only for storage.

But there was a new, ten-second recording waiting for me. I have only watched it once, and I know if I look at it again, my mind will completely break.

The footage showed her old bedroom. It was dark, silent, and completely barren for the first nine seconds of the clip. Then, right at the final second, something slowly leaned into the camera frame from the far corner of the ceiling. It was a shape, warped and elongated, wearing my daughter's exact face. It looked directly into the camera lens and flashed a wide, unblinking, impossible smile.

And right before the video cut to black, it whispered:

"She never made it home."

Behind the old bowling alley, there is a building on the side of the hill. It’s a small, run-down cabin only hidden by a few sparse trees. Some days when I go out to smoke, I just stare at it.

I didn't think much of it until I asked one of my coworkers. She got this serious look on her face and went completely silent. After a few seconds, she just took a long sip of her beer and shook her head. Anytime I tried to push further, she was quick to shut me down.

Later that weekend, I tried to ask my friend Levi, who had lived in the town his whole life. He was normally such a happy, carefree guy, but his face turned nearly white when I asked him. He tried to change the conversation. When I pushed him on it, he said, “It’s a place where bad shit happens. Promise me you won’t go there- I have to hear you say you promise.” Seeing how serious he was, I promised, albeit hesitantly. He acted off the rest of the night, leaving early because he had something come up at the last minute.

Even with what Levi had said, I had to go find out for myself. I had to see it, even if it was nothing, even if it was dangerous- I just had to know.

When night came, I told my dad I was gonna get food. He nodded, barely looking up from the scattered paperwork and beer bottles that littered his desk. I watched him for a moment before I left for the cabin. When I got there, I made my way down the hill and across the creek. The area around the cabin was silent, no crickets, no birds, nothing.

I stood at the front of the cabin. The wood warped and darkened. I traced the outside with my flashlight. It was small, probably no more than two or three rooms. I looked down at the cracked wood on the stairs leading up to the porch. I placed my foot on one step and pushed the wood slightly. It creaked, but held well under the weight.

I stepped onto the porch, which had a single rocking chair, swaying slightly in the faint wind. I stepped up to the wooden door and stood there for nearly a full minute. A part of me wanted to go back, the rational part of my brain telling me that whatever was in here wasn’t worth it. But a bigger part of me had to know what scared people so much about this old place.

A wooden chair had been wedged beneath the handle, blocking the door from the outside. I moved it aside and pushed the door slightly. It squeaked loudly against the heavily rusted hinges.

I shone my flashlight inside. The place still had old furniture that looked completely untouched, all covered in a layer of dust. There was an old wooden bed, a small bedside table, and a moldy red carpet. I took a step inside, propping the door open with the chair. The air inside was still, my flashlight illuminating the dust particles floating in the air.

I looked over to the door to my left. It was closed, the walls next to it adorned with paintings I didn’t recognize. I walked over to the door and gave it a soft push, as it creaked open. I shone my flashlight through the doorway.

I stopped, nearly dropping my flashlight as my heart sank to my feet and my stomach churned.

On the opposite side of the room, something impossibly large was crouched against the wall.

My heart raced as I stared at it. I took a slow, careful step backward before bumping into the door. I jumped at the sudden contact, dropping the flashlight as it clattered to the floor, illuminating the thing in a sickening light.

I whipped around, about to run as far as I could before a pungent scent cut through the air, filling my nostrils. It smelled exactly like the fudge that my mom made for Christmas. It was something I hadn’t smelt in so long. I slowly turned around, facing the thing on the other side of the cramped room. The hair hanging from its face stirred, the rest of its body as still as stone.

The smell wafted through the air, latching onto me like an invisible rope. Against my better judgment, I took a step towards it. The hair on its face rustled as its lower jaw began to drop, popping and cracking as it stretched until it hit the floor.

I walked up to it until it was towering above me. I stared into its maw, a tunnel made of old flesh. It had two rows of flat teeth on its lower jaw that, like pigs fighting for food, pushed against each other.

As I got closer, I realized something. The smell was coming from inside its throat. I saw a glint of something peeking out from behind its matted hair.

It was an eye.

Staring directly at me.

My body tightened. I had to run to get as far away from here as possible and never return. I took a deep breath- and I smelled it again. The sweet smell of freshly made fudge. The memory of her was so warm that it was hard to fight against it. I turned my head back down as I gazed into its mouth. It was more repulsive than anything I’d ever seen in my life— but it smelled so nice, so comforting.

Before I realized it, I had stepped into its mouth. My shoe sank into its tongue, making a sickening squelch. The inside was covered in dark blood and various, frantic scratch marks. I looked down at its massive, crooked teeth. They were the size of dinner plates, yellowed and covered in what looked like dried blood.

It did not react.

Its throat stretched, a deep, convulsing tunnel that seemed to go on forever.

It smelled so sweet. Now that I was closer, I could smell it so clearly. I closed my eyes and pictured the homemade bars of whipped fudge, topped with crushed bits of peppermint. I could picture my mother smiling as she handed them to me. I felt myself smile.

I took another step.

I pushed against the saliva-covered walls. My hands were almost sticking to the tacky, slick flesh.

I got on my hands and knees and began crawling. Its mouth was slimy, covered in thick, viscous saliva. I could hear it breathing around me, deep, low breaths that sounded more like a building settling than any living creature. It was calm, remaining patiently still.

I saw the light behind me slowly disappear as its mouth closed. I couldn’t go back, nor did I want to. I merely just kept crawling further. Its throat began to constrict around me. My clothes began to rip and tear against the pressure. I couldn’t do anything but pull myself forward.

I heard a loud pop as my leg snapped in two, tearing open my skin like wet cloth. The pain was unbearable. I stopped momentarily before clenching my teeth, using the only leg I had to push myself forward, deeper into it.

I was so close, I could feel it. If I just kept crawling, I might be able to remember what she looked like, the way she laughed, the way she smiled when she looked at Dad and me.

Things I had not seen in so, so long.

I lost feeling in my legs, pulling myself forward with my hands, my nails scraping against the walls of its slimy throat.

Each desperate pull only moved me a few centimeters, but I could do nothing else but continue to move. I used what hollow strength I had to push against it as I crawled forward. With each pulse of its throat, I felt my grip loosen.

I felt an intense pressure build up around my chest, squeezing me until I felt my ribs begin to snap. I felt one of them tear into my lungs as all the air rushed out of me.

My arms dropped, pushed together, then folded backward over my elbow with a loud pop as I felt blood pour out of the fresh wound. Every ounce of strength left my body as I screamed; the sound muffled against the breathing walls.

Something sweet began to pool in my mouth as my vision blurred.

It tasted like fudge.

Posting on a throwaway account because there's a chance I'm being watched.

I'm a security guard for a local library. I usually take night patrols and closing rounds due to my insomnia, which has been worse lately. Nothing weird ever happened on the job, the problem is the apartment above mine.

On quiet nights I come back around 11:30 pm, if some alarm goes off or someone is seen around the property after closing time, I only get home at 2 am, sometimes even later.

A few weeks back we had a problem with a homeless person so I had to stay late until the cops arrived. When I got to my room it was well past midnight. That's when the noises started. It was only some music at first, a bit odd for the time but I just kept brewing my middle of the night coffee.

Then a thud happened. The ceiling trembled for a brief moment. Something fell down on the apartment above, I've never been more sure of something in my life. I instantly turned off my coffee machine. Now that I could hear things properly, the music had stopped.

For a few minutes I just stood there, paralyzed by the silence. A swarm of footsteps erupted all at once. They were frantic, too many to count. Before I could try anything, I heard the door above being unlocked as people rushed down the stairs. I couldn't bring myself to open my door until the sun was fully out.

Nothing else happened for many days. I started to think my imagination just got carried away. Wouldn't be the first time my insomnia got the best of me. Still, something seemed off. I realized that I had never seen nor heard my upstairs neighbor once in my two years living here. My attention got focused on catching any signs that someone actually lived there and I wasn't going insane.

Nothing. Not a single sound came from upstairs.

After speaking to other neighbors in hopes of getting some closure, I only grew more confused. No one had ever seen the person in apartment 702. Worst of all, no one heard any of what I heard that night.

So I moved on, and accepted that I was just imagining things due to my lack of sleep. But I found something that made me make this post, I don't know what else to do.

My laptop was getting a full storage warning even though I didn't use it for anything other than browsing youtube and watching movies. I spent an entire afternoon just checking as many folders as I could, but I couldn't find anything that would occupy half a terabyte of space.

The next day, I watched some videos about clearing your storage properly and found out about hidden files. All I had to do was check a view option, 'Show hidden files, folders and drives'. I applied the change and suddenly, it appeared. A single hidden folder on my desktop titled '702'.

My heart's drumming became so loud I could barely hear anything. Slowly, I lifted my head and looked around to make sure my only company was my empty room. I clicked on the folder. I've never had a heart attack before but if anything felt like one, this was it.

Dozens of videos. Each one with a different length. Some were five minutes long, others were twenty. I looked around my room one more time. Nothing. It's just me here. I kept repeating that in my head as I opened the first video.

A completely still, far away shot, pointed towards the 702 apartment door. I sped the video up to see if anything happens. At the seven minute mark the door starts moving. A man with a suit and sun glasses comes out. His hair is short, jet black, just like his suit. His skin is extremely pale and the clothing seems expensive but it's hard to tell finer details with footage this grainy. Zooming in does nothing except making everything look worse.

The man goes downstairs while the camera is still fixated at the door. Something below the 702 apartment moves. My door. I go up the stairs so slowly it looks like I'm about to crawl. As I stand in front of 702, I look back and stare directly at the camera. The video ends.

I immediately click on the second video.

It's inside an apartment. Poorly lit, but I could see walls and furniture through their silhouettes. The camera stops and stares at certain objects randomly. Landline phone, Table full of tangled cables, Empty kitchen drawers and an oak door. A hand tries to open it. My hand, I think. It was locked, the video ends abruptly.

I went through as many videos as I could. Speeding them up, skimming the preview and sometimes skipping ahead. Most of them are the same still shot of the 702 door but on different days. Except for the last one.

It's inside an apartment again, the same one. This time the person holding the camera walks through the dim spaces without stopping, until they get to the oak door. They freeze for a second, heavy breathing seeps through the quiet as the view starts to get lower and lower, finally reaching floor level.

The camera lingers for a bit. Then, a green filter takes over. Heavy contrast of different grey hues make the apartment fully visible, including the gap underneath the door. It moves forward with a steady rhythm and as it reaches the other side, it gets blinded by bright lights.

The filter turns off, revealing a multitude of screens. White lines moving non stop in some, while others appear static. PC cases on the floor blink colored dots, their whirling taking over the entire room.

A distant chunk of metal jolts. The video ends.

I don't understand why, but I felt an intense urge to check the 702 apartment in that moment. I closed the laptop, put my shoes on and got my pepper spray.

I opened my door, my mouth was dry and my throat hoarse. I crept up the steps trying to keep the stillness around me, It was almost 3 am. As I stood in front of 702, I looked back, all I could see was the empty hall leading to the elevator. I faced forward again, staring at the number directly.

I lowered to the floor slowly, hearing every creak it had to give. I couldn't see anything through the gap, so I kept getting closer. When my forehead was about to touch the door, a stench hit me. It smelled like copper mixed with rot. My head knocked back. All I could do was try to stop my gagging.

I can still feel the hairs on my neck standing. Dread feels as if it's trying to gnaw through the lining of my stomach. Every fiber of my being in this moment is telling me to run, yet I am paralysed. I noticed my vision shaking only to realize I’d been holding my breath. For how long, I couldn’t tell, but I found myself gasping for the next breath of fresh air.  
I peeled back the sheets and slowly stepped out of bed. The icy cold contact of the floor grounds me. Still nothing. What could have awoken me and left me in such a wretched condition? It is quite demoralizing to find yourself reduced to the same fears as a lone toddler who had only just begun to stray from their mother's side. With this in mind, I probed the room top to bottom once more before concluding that there was no threat at hand. Feeling at ease, I crawled back into bed. The sheets were still soaked through with sweat, but that would be a problem for tomorrow, I thought, until blood was roaring in my ears once more, and that gnawing feeling of dread ripped its way into my throat. I heard this time,

“Thomas”

A voice of rot and atrophy whispered. My gaze jerks around the room unevenly until it rests upon the painting hanging on the adjacent wall. I must be losing my mind, I quickly deny until,  
“Thomas”, the voice full of filth echoes.

I stare.

“It would be wise to stay inside tomorrow.”  
It offers.

I stare, studying the painting. I’m still not sure what’s happening right now. I must be dreaming. I never thought I could be so still. It was as if every fiber of my being would be agonized simply at the thought of moving. The painting offered nothing else in the period I sat frozen in wait, and yet I am sure that vile thing had said my name. Much more than that, was it threatening me? Had it given a warning? Curiosity guided my timid approach, and I attempted to steer my gaze in a way that would still make escape possible. The painting. It’s just that. Left to me from an unknown relative. He’s dressed poorly and is obviously in a state of decay, yet there is a bounty of food and guests surrounding him. It’s difficult to say what event is being portrayed, but the spectator’s expressions carry screams of delirium. I cringed backward after realizing my sudden engrossment in this display had left me peering mere inches away from it. As if it were able to reach out and grab me, I nervously laugh to myself. “It would be wise to stay inside tomorrow.”  
My gaze locks on the painting. It's still mute.  
Brushing off the sinking feeling in my stomach, my morning continues as usual. While walking out the door, my eyes meet with the painting one last time. “Don't go out there, you'll die.”

I know every sound this house makes. I have lived here thirty-one years, and in that time the building has confessed everything to me — the arthritic click of the radiator at half past two, the low moan the kitchen window makes when the wind comes from the north, the third step on the staircase that groans under weight like a man reluctant to admit pain. I know these sounds the way I know my own breathing. Unconsciously. Completely.

That is why, on the night this began, I did not get out of bed.

It was the third step. That particular complaint, that low and specific creak — I heard it from my room at the end of the hall, and I lay still, and I thought: the house is settling. Houses settle. Thirty-one years and I have never once been afraid of a sound I could name.  
I named it. I closed my eyes.  
I listened to the silence that followed and I thought nothing of it.  
· · ·  
The second night, it happened again.  
Third step. That same reluctant confession. And then — as before — nothing. No fourth step. No fifth. Only the sound of my own heart, which had, without my permission, begun to move a little faster.  
I told myself: an animal had found a way in. A raccoon, perhaps, displaced by the weather. They are clever with old houses. They know the unlocked places.  
I did not go to check. I want to be honest about that. I did not go to check, and I cannot now pretend it was because I was certain. I did not go because some part of me — the part that has survived this long by listening to itself — did not want to know what it would find at the bottom of the stairs.  
I lay in the dark and I counted my breaths and eventually morning arrived, pale and indifferent, and I went downstairs and found nothing. No animal. No disturbance. Only the house, guileless in daylight, offering me its ordinary face.  
I made coffee. I did not look at the third step.  
· · ·  
By the fifth night I had developed a system. I would lie very still — not rigid, not braced, but still in the way of water before a stone enters it. And I would listen. And the third step would speak, and then the silence would fall, and I would count.  
One. Two. Three.  
On what I believe was the ninth night, I counted to forty before I slept.  
The thing I cannot explain — the thing I have tried to explain to no one, because there is no version of this that does not sound like the unraveling of a particular kind of mind — is that the silence was not empty. You understand the difference, I think, between a house that is quiet and a house in which something is holding its breath. One is the absence of sound. The other is the presence of waiting.  
My house had become the second kind.  
· · ·  
I called my sister on the eleventh day. I told her I hadn't been sleeping well. She asked if I wanted company. I said no before I had finished hearing the offer.  
I asked her, carefully, as though it were an idle question, whether she had ever noticed anything strange about the house on her visits. She said she'd always found it a little cold. I asked what she meant. She said: cold. You know. A little cold. The way some rooms are.  
I did not tell her that no room in my house had ever been cold before this month. I did not tell her that the temperature near the foot of the stairs had dropped by what felt like ten degrees, and that I had been taking a longer route through the kitchen to avoid walking past it.  
I thanked her and hung up and stood in the kitchen for a very long time.  
The third step creaked at 2:17 in the afternoon, while I was standing six feet away from it, holding a cup of coffee, in full daylight, completely alone.  
I did not spill the coffee. I am proud of that, in the useless way one is proud of small dignities in undignified moments. I set the cup down on the counter with both hands and I walked — I did not run — I walked to the front door and I stood outside in the cold for eleven minutes.  
When I came back inside, I did not look at the staircase.  
I have not looked directly at it since.  
· · ·  
I sleep downstairs now. I tell myself it is temporary.  
Last night I woke at — I think it was just past two, the clock on the microwave said 2:19 — to the sound of the third step, and then the fourth step, and then the fifth, and then the slow and careful and deliberate progression of something that had apparently decided it was done waiting at the bottom of the stairs.  
I lay very still on the sofa. I watched the hallway doorway, which was dark.  
The footsteps stopped outside the living room. There was, for a long time, nothing — that weighted, breathing silence I have come to know — and then they resumed, retreating, back down the hall, back to the staircase, ascending, until the house was quiet again.  
I did not sleep. I waited for morning with my eyes on the doorway and my hands folded on my chest like a woman already practicing for something.  
I am writing this down because I think it is important to have a record. Because I am still, in some department of myself, a rational person who believes in documentation. Because if someone finds this, I want them to understand that I heard everything. I understood what I was hearing. I made the choice, each night, to stay.  
I don't know why I stayed.  
That is not true.  
I stayed because on the twelfth night — before it learned to come downstairs — I heard the third step creak, and then the silence, and then, barely, barely audible, something I have not written until this moment and cannot fully write even now: a sound from just outside my bedroom door. Not a knock. Not a scratch. Something lower, and slower, and more patient than either of those things. Something that sounded, impossibly, like my name.  
And the voice — if voice is the right word for it, which I don't believe it is — the voice was familiar.  
It was familiar in the way that a reflection is familiar. In the way that the third step is familiar. In the way that thirty-one years in one house makes everything familiar, makes you believe you have heard everything this building will ever say to you, have learned its whole vocabulary of sounds.  
It is tonight, and the house is quiet, and in a moment I am going to get up and I am going to walk to the staircase and I am going to look at the third step.  
I need to know if there is anything on it.  
I need to know what has been standing there.  
I have not told you the one detail that I have been circling all along, the one I keep arriving at and turning away from like a doorway I'm not ready to enter — which is that my bedroom is at the end of the hall, and the sofa where I sleep now is directly below it, and last night, when the footsteps stopped and the silence came, what I heard from the ceiling above me was not nothing.  
What I heard from the ceiling above me was the sound of someone getting into my bed.  
The mattress springs. The specific compression and sigh of weight settling in.  
And then the sound of breathing — slow, slow, regular — the sound of something making itself comfortable.  
The sound of something going to sleep.  
It is quiet now. The house has been quiet for hours. I am going to the stairs.  
I want you to know that I am not afraid. I want you to know that I have lived here thirty-one years. I want you to know that I am going because I have decided that not-knowing is its own kind of horror, and I am choosing this one instead.  
The third step will tell me everything.  
It always does.

The wind howled loudly as the waves beat against the small boat. Paul gripped at the wheel tightly. Slowly guiding them back to land. He felt like he would fall any second with how much the small boat was rocking.

Almost there, he thought. He would be happy to climb into a nice warm bed at the inn and fall asleep. God he didn't think he had ever been warm at sea.

Paul could feel his eyes getting heavier. Maybe he should wake up one of the other guys and take a break. His hands slacked on the wheel for a second, his eyes closed shut.

He felt a sudden lurch. His eyes sprung back open. Fully alert. His eyes focused on the window. He saw a huge figure in the water. But it couldn't be there, it was normally so much further out at sea. He turned the wheel abruptly but it was too late.

Bang!

He slammed into the side. His chest aching.

“Hey lad. What was that? What happened?” Dan asked from behind him, his face worried and panicked.

“Sorry it was my fault.” Paul mumbled back.

“Hey guys. I don't want to alarm anyone, but I think we're sinking.” Spoke a third voice.

Paul pinched the bridge of his nose. God, could this night get any worse.

His eyes rising, he looked out at the tall solid figure in the water in front of them. The lighthouse. He could have sworn it was supposed to be further out in the sea.

His eyes trailed up the tall and imposing building.

“Do you think there's someone in there?” He asked.

“Maybe lad. Might be our best bet. Can't stay here. Come on. Let's find out.” Dan replied.

The three of them move towards the door. Grabbing their jackets on the way out and quickly sliding their shoes on.

They carefully climbed from their little boat to the lighthouse rocks.

“Mind your step. It's awful out here!” Dan yelled. The weather, beating down on their leather jackets. They were soaked to the bone in seconds.

They carefully made it across the slippery rocks.

“Hey the door. It's open.” Paul yelled, being the first of the three to make it over.

They slowly made it inside. Paul felt a little wary about the situation. Why would the door be open in a storm?

“Hello” he called. His voice echoed.

The wind howled outside as they made their way further inside. Water dropped repetitively from somewhere.

“I don't think anyone is here lad.” Dan spoke from behind him.

Paul opened his mouth to respond.

“I'm here.” A figure spoke in the shadows.

The three of them looked at where the voice had come from. A man. Young. Early 20s.

He walked out from the shadows.

“Are you fellows alright? I saw you out in the storm.” He spoke.

“We're fine. A bit shaken. Could we stay here till rescue comes.” Paul asked hopefully.

“You may stay the night, if you wish.” The man spoke.

“Yeah, thanks. That would be very helpful.” Paul responded.

“Great. Yes you must stay, let’s go upstairs.” The keeper spoke

The four of them made it up the stairs. Ben suddenly gripped Dan’s arm to hold him back.

“What is it lad?” Dan asked.

In a whisper Ben spoke.

“Don't you think he looks old? Like his clothes?” He asked.

“Well some people like to dress like that. Nothing wrong with that.” Dan dismissed and continued to follow the others up the stairs.

They continue up the steep steps slowly making their way to the top.

“Just through here, gentleman.” The keeper spoke as he guided them to a small sitting area. The fire lit and chairs neatly arranged in the area. The men all sat finally glad to be safe and warm. Paul couldn’t believe how lucky they were that someone was home.

“So are you the only one here?” Paul asked curiously.

“Yes, just me. I like a quiet life. You will stay won't you?” The keeper asked again, his eyes focused intently on Paul. Paul noticed then how still the man was. His eyes barely blinked as he looked at him.

“I told you we would.” He replied, unease began to fill him.

“Good. Good” the keeper muttered, a smile suddenly appearing on his face, but Paul noticed that this smile did not match his eyes. He stood in front of them in a frozen state, just staring and smiling.

“So…. Do you have any food? We're starving. If it's not too much trouble.” Paul asked, trying to break the tension a little. It’s just a strange man cut off from the world, he thought.

“Oh of course. I have biscuits somewhere. Anything for the people that will stay.” The keeper replied, finally moving off and disappearing into the kitchen area.

A little strange, Paul thought nothing more.

“Have you seen him blink once? Because I haven't.” Ben spoke in a whisper. Paul turned to him. So he hadn’t been the only one to notice.

“He’s on his own, makes people a bit strange.” Paul responded.

“Yeah strange, but this is weird. Don’t you think Dan?” Ben asked.

“Haven't been paying that much attention lad. Just glad to be out of that weather. It's nice here.” Replied Dan dismissively.

Just then the keeper returned a tin in his hand.

“Here friends.” He spoke, handing the tin out.

Ben reached for it. The keeper retreated into the shadows.

“Oh great custard creams, my favourite.” Ben spoke excitedly.

They all reached into the tin pulling out a handful each and began to munch on them. God they tasted so good, Paul thought.

Paul reached in for another having just finished the four in his hand. One more, he thought, then he was done.

He grabbed the biscuits and slowly bit into it.

Hard.

This one tastes weird, he thought

Like it had been left out too long. Stale.

He pulled it away from his mouth and looked at it. Now he was staring at it. It looked dusty, it crumbled in his hand.

He looked up from his biscuit and looked at the keeper. Who stood half hidden, that smile on his face had reappeared. If he hadn't spoken to him earlier he would have swore he was a statue. Something was wrong here, Paul thought. Fear spiked through him. Maybe he was being silly though. It's just a strange person.

"Hey, I didn't know this place had a keeper. Now that I think about it I haven't heard of this place having a new one. Are you the family of the old one?" He asked, trying to get some answers out of the man.

"There is no keeper here. You must stay, won't you." The man spoke, his voice sounded different, hollow. That was all Paul needed, he sprung to his feet dropping the biscuit tin in the process, the tin hit the floor loudly and the leftover biscuits fell out.

"Get up. Now. Come on. Back downstairs. Now" Paul could feel it. Utter terror gripped his body. The other two had also discarded the food standing up at Paul’s frantic voice.

They rushed for the staircase. The panic on all of their faces.

Paul turned to face the room for a second. It looked old all of a sudden. The seats were broken, and the fire. The fire had gone out. A chill went up his spine.

Paul also noticed that the man hadn't moved at all. Something was very wrong here, he thought as he ran down the stairs behind his ship mates

The staircase felt like they got through it too fast. Weren't they longer going up? Paul was breathing heavily, his breath so cold you could see it.

“Lad! There's no door! I. I can't find it. Paul! The door. Where was it?” Dan yelled, being the first one to reach it.

Paul looked frantically. They had definitely come in here. He remembered it being open. Inviting.

“It was here. Right here.” He said his voice shaking as he reached out with his hands. Come on, please, he thought.

Footsteps echoed behind him. The noise, the loudest thing in the room.

Please God, please. Paul thought.

“You will stay.” The voice spoke. More distorted than ever.

There was no hope.

The keeper had caught them.

I have a strange habit. Every night before I go to bed, I check my apartment door exactly once. Not twice. Not three times. Once.

Years ago, a roommate pointed out how often I checked locks. He said I would stand there turning the deadbolt over and over until I was satisfied. I hated how ridiculous it sounded, so I forced myself to stop. Since then, I lock the door, test the handle one time, and walk away. No exceptions.

Three months ago, I came home from work and found my apartment door unlocked. I remember standing there in the hallway staring at it. I knew I had locked it that morning. I remembered the sound of the deadbolt sliding into place. Nothing appeared stolen. Nothing looked disturbed. Eventually I convinced myself that I had simply forgotten.

Two days later it happened again. The door was unlocked. This time I searched the entire apartment. Closets. Bathroom. Under the bed. Nobody was there. As I was about to give up, I noticed something sitting beside the kitchen sink. A blue coffee mug. I didn't own a blue coffee mug. It had a chipped handle and a faded logo I couldn't recognize. I threw it into the trash before going to bed. The next morning it was back. Sitting exactly where I had found it. That was when I started getting nervous.

Over the following weeks, more things changed. A chair would be facing the wrong direction. A lamp I had switched off would be glowing when I got home. Books moved between shelves. A framed photograph appeared on the wrong wall. None of it was dramatic. Nothing valuable disappeared. The changes were so small that I struggled to explain them to anyone else. But they kept happening. Every single week. I stopped inviting people over. I stopped sleeping properly. I began checking every room before bed.

One night I woke up around three in the morning. The room was completely dark. At first I thought I had imagined it. Then I heard breathing. Slow. Steady. Close. Not outside. Not in another room. Inside my bedroom. I lay frozen beneath the blankets. The breathing continued for several seconds. Then it stopped. I reached for the lamp and switched it on. The room was empty. Nobody stood near my bed. Nobody hid in the corners. Nothing looked unusual. I didn't sleep for the rest of the night.

The next day I bought a security camera. I mounted it on a shelf facing my bedroom door. For six nights the footage showed nothing unusual. On the seventh night, I found something that made my blood run cold. At 2:14 AM, my bedroom door slowly opened. A man stepped inside. At first I thought he was a stranger. Then he moved closer to the camera. The same face. The same hair. The same scar beneath my chin. He looked exactly like me. I watched the footage in complete silence. The man walked to the side of my bed and stood there. Watching me sleep. Not speaking. Not moving. Just staring. The timestamp continued counting upward. One minute. Five minutes. Ten minutes. Twenty-three minutes. Then he quietly turned around and left. I watched the video six times before calling the police.

They found nothing. No fingerprints. No signs of forced entry. No evidence. One officer suggested it was an edited recording. Another suggested I might know the man. I stopped arguing. I knew what I had seen.

After that, I started noticing him everywhere. Across the street while I walked home from work. At train stations. In store windows. Always watching. Always waiting. Whenever I tried to approach him, he disappeared. I became obsessed. I started carrying my phone everywhere. I took photographs whenever I thought I saw him. I filled folders with blurry images. Reflections. Crowds. Shadows. Every picture seemed to contain someone who looked almost exactly like me.

The obsession consumed my life. Then, last week, I noticed something strange. I was reviewing one of the photographs. The image showed the reflection of a storefront window. The man was standing inside the reflection. Watching me. I almost deleted it. Then I noticed the date. The timestamp was wrong. According to my phone, the picture had been taken four years earlier. That was impossible. I didn't even live in this city four years ago. I assumed it was a software error. Then I checked the rest. Another image. Five years old. Another. Three years old. Another. Six years old. Every photograph containing the man had a timestamp from before I moved here. Before I rented the apartment. Before I even had this phone.

I stopped sleeping entirely after that. Two nights ago, I searched through the apartment for answers. I pulled books off shelves. Opened drawers. Emptied closets. At the back of a kitchen cabinet, hidden behind a loose panel, I found a folder. Inside were documents. Utility bills. Insurance papers. A lease agreement. All belonging to the previous tenant. The name meant nothing to me. Until I found the photograph. My hands started shaking immediately. The man in the picture was smiling at the camera. He had my face. My scar. My eyes. Everything. The photograph had been taken seven years ago. I had never seen it before.

I spent the next hour staring at old documents. The same name appeared everywhere. The previous tenant. The man who had lived here before me. The man who looked exactly like me. Then I noticed something written on the back of the photograph. A date. And a sentence. The date was seven years old. The sentence was worse. It read: "If you're reading this, he sees you now."

Yesterday I reviewed the security footage one final time. I don't know why. Maybe I wanted proof that I wasn't losing my mind. Maybe I wanted one mistake. One detail that would prove all of this was fake. Instead I found something worse. Something I hadn't noticed before. The timestamp. The footage showing the man standing beside my bed wasn't recorded last month. It wasn't recorded this year. It wasn't even recorded after I moved in. The video was seven years old. Seven. The man standing beside the bed wasn't watching me. He was watching the previous tenant. The one in the photograph. The one with my face. The one who left the warning.

I sat there staring at the screen for almost an hour. Then I noticed movement in the reflection of my monitor. Someone was standing behind my chair. Watching me. I already knew what I would see before I turned around. The scar beneath his chin matched mine perfectly. But for the first time, I noticed something else. He wasn't copying me. I was copying him.

I did not sleep. I waited for morning with my eyes on the doorway and my hands folded on my chest like a woman already practicing for something.

I am writing this down because I think it is important to have a record. Because I am still, in some department of myself, a rational person who believes in documentation. Because if someone finds this, I want them to understand that I heard everything. I understood what I was hearing. I made the choice, each night, to stay.

I don’t know why I stayed.

That is not true.

I stayed because on the twelfth night — before it learned to come downstairs — I heard the third step creak, and then the silence, and then, barely, barely audible, something I have not written until this moment and cannot fully write even now: a sound from just outside my bedroom door. Not a knock. Not a scratch. Something lower, and slower, and more patient than either of those things. Something that sounded, impossibly, like my name.

And the voice — if voice is the right word for it, which I don’t believe it is — the voice was familiar.

It was familiar in the way that a reflection is familiar. In the way that the third step is familiar. In the way that thirty-one years in one house makes everything familiar, makes you believe you have heard everything this building will ever say to you, have learned its whole vocabulary of sounds.

It is tonight, and the house is quiet, and in a moment I am going to get up and I am going to walk to the staircase and I am going to look at the third step.

I need to know if there is anything on it.

I need to know what has been standing there.

I have not told you the one detail that I have been circling all along, the one I keep arriving at and turning away from like a doorway I’m not ready to enter — which is that my bedroom is at the end of the hall, and the sofa where I sleep now is directly below it, and last night, when the footsteps stopped and the silence came, what I heard from the ceiling above me was not nothing.

What I heard from the ceiling above me was the sound of someone getting into my bed.

The mattress springs. The specific compression and sigh of weight settling in.

And then the sound of breathing — slow, slow, regular — the sound of something making itself comfortable.

The sound of something going to sleep.

It is quiet now. The house has been quiet for hours. I am going to the stairs.

I want you to know that I am not afraid. I want you to know that I have lived here thirty-one years. I want you to know that I am going because I have decided that not-knowing is its own kind of horror, and I am choosing this one instead.

The third step will tell me everything.

It always does.
