End

Written by Vinicius Dutra

The first scream doesn’t sound human.

It slices through the bass rattling my dashboard, a raw wire of sound that makes my skin prickle. Halloween night—fog machines coughing over lawns, skeletons twitching to motion sensors, kids shrieking in sugar-fueled hysteria. Every driveway’s an echo chamber of laughter and cheap horror. I’m just a rideshare driver counting the last run of the night before I get home. Then my app chimes: Arrived.

Only… there’s no passenger.

The fog thickens. The street smells like burned leaves and fake fog juice, and in that split second between beats, another scream shatters the music. This one isn’t playful—it’s sharp, like glass dragged over tile.

A small figure bolts out of the space between two houses. A little girl in a tinfoil crown, silver duct-tape dress fluttering like peeling skin. She trips over a gravestone prop and hits my passenger door so hard my rearview mirror shakes.

“Open!” she cries, slamming her hands against the window. “Please—please—open the door!”

No one turns. The crowd keeps laughing, the plastic reaper keeps cackling, the houses keep smiling. Someone yells, “Nice acting!” while I hit the unlock button.

She dives in the moment the lock clicks. The smell of iron and sweat hits me before I see the blood streaking her arm. It’s thin, steady, real.

“Go!” she gasps, eyes fixed behind us. “Drive. Now.”

I don’t ask questions. I slam the gas. Tires squeal, fake cobwebs tear off a mailbox. I catch movement in the mirror—three figures stepping out from the dark. Hoodies. Skull masks. Glitter catching in the headlights like shards of bone. They don’t run. They glide, slow and sure, as if they already know where I’ll turn.

“Who are they?” I ask, knuckles white on the wheel.

“They saw me,” she whispers. “I had to get off the line.”

“What line?”

She points. The headlights catch strips of orange tape running along every porch, mailboxes, fences—one unbroken artery glowing faint in the mist.

The longer I look, the more the air hums. My GPS glitches—the road lines ripple and twist, curling around the cul-de-sac like a noose tightening.

“What’s your name?” I manage.

“Nora.” Her voice is a breath. “It’s 11:41. We have to move. Midnight’s when it takes the mask off.”

“The mask?”

She doesn’t answer. The laughter outside fades into distance, replaced by wind dragging plastic decorations across asphalt. Every porch light flickers, fighting to stay alive.

At 11:46, everything dies.

Not dim. Not off. Gone.

Fog swallows the world. Inflatable pumpkins deflate in a synchronized sigh. A thousand tiny electric eyes blink out. The quiet that follows has weight—it presses on the chest. I can hear my heartbeat in my ears.

“Keep driving,” Nora says. Her voice is trembling. “Don’t stop for anyone.”

A man in a werewolf costume stumbles into the street, waving a phone. I swerve to miss him. He turns toward the headlights, and his face—God—his face is blank. Smooth skin stretched where features should be. The fur on his collar smokes under my lights as I pass.

11:50. My phone buzzes. Emergency alert.

UNAUTHORIZED EMERGENCY flashes in crimson before the screen dies. The speakers crackle, hissing with static. Then a voice slides through—breathy, layered—whispering something I shouldn’t understand but do.

My name.

Nora clutches her ears. “It uses what connects us. Wires. Waves. Sound.”

“The what?”

“The rule.”

My grip slips on the wheel. “What happens at midnight?”

“It chooses,” she says.

The GPS redraws itself, every route curling inward like veins collapsing toward a single, pulsing heart. The orange line glows brighter—alive beneath the pavement.

“Left,” she orders. “Then right. Then left again. We have to reach the dead subdivision. The line forgot to finish there.”

We drive into silence. The neighborhood unravels. Streetlights vanish. Houses thin out into skeletons of framing and plywood. Signs rot where lawns should be. The night feels unfinished—like someone stopped building reality halfway.

“Stop,” she whispers.

The tape ends at the curb like a severed artery.

Nora exhales shakily. “If you cross here, you’re free. But if I come with you… it follows. Always.”

“What are you talking about?”

“Every year,” she says, eyes wet and fever-bright, “one person steps on the line after eleven. One keeps it full. The town stays safe. That’s the rule.”

“They feed it?”

Her nod is small. “It prefers the ones who stop.”

I feel the blood drain from my face. I stopped. I opened the door.

Nora looks down. “If I go back, it’ll take me instead. If you don’t let me, it’ll take us both.”

11:58.

The air outside rustles, heavy. Something moves—fabric dragging, nails on concrete. The windows vibrate as if something’s breathing against them. I swear every shadow has eyes.

“Nora—”

She opens the door. Cold air floods in, smelling like rain on metal. “I’m sorry. But you saved me. That means something.”

I grab her wrist. “You don’t have to—”

She looks at me, hollow-eyed. “Neither do you.”

11:59.

I don’t think. I kill the engine and step out.

The world shifts. The ground hums—a low, living vibration. The fog congeals, hardening into shape. Houses rise out of shadow, ribs and doorframes glowing orange at the edges. Porch lights flare to life one by one, staring down like eyes opening for the first time.

Then the knock.

Three slow hits. Deep. Heavy. Not on wood. On the world.

Nora’s hand slips into mine. Her pulse stutters like a trapped bird. “We’re off the line,” she whispers. “Run.”

We run.

The air stretches, warps, claws at us. The dark tries to make walls, doorways, cages. Behind us—footsteps? No, scraping, wet and deliberate. Something laughs through static. My lungs burn, but I don’t look back.

Then—headlights. Real. Blinding. The highway.

We crash through a ditch, stumble onto gravel, choking on cold air. The sound behind us dies mid-breath.

Nora drops to her knees. “We made it.”

My phone pings. Signal. Normal. The emergency alert gone, replaced by the dull quiet hum of traffic.

We stand trembling under the streetlight. Down the ramp, a gas station hums in sterile brightness. People move inside, unaware. Safe.

“You coming?” I ask.

She hesitates. “If I go back, it can’t follow you.”

“And if you don’t?”

“I don’t know.”

The night holds its breath.

I take her hand again. “Then you’ll find out with me.”

She blinks. Then nods.

We walk down together. The automatic door slides open. Warm air spills over us, bright and humming. The cashier’s eyes widen.

“Y’all okay?”

Nora beats me to it. “We will be.”

Behind us, far away, the town exhales. One by one, porch lights flicker back on. The orange tape gleams anew. And somewhere deep under it all—three heavy knocks echo again.

The rule resets.

And waits for next Halloween.

I was desperate. Bills, my mom’s medical debt, the kind of exhaustion that makes minimum wage sound luxurious. The ad promised $28 an hour for solitude. Perfect. The gym sits in an old meat-packing warehouse on the edge of [redacted]. No natural light in the back. The air always tastes faintly of copper and sweat no matter how much ozone the machines pump out.

Marcus interviewed me during daylight hours. He was too tall, veins crawling like living cables under skin stretched too tight. His handshake felt like it wanted to test my grip strength. He smiled with too many teeth and said, “The building rewards dedication. Just follow the protocols.”

He handed me the keycard and left me alone with the sheet bolted to the staff room wall.

IRON ETERNAL – NIGHT SHIFT PROTOCOLS

11 PM – 6 AM. Break them and become part of the gains.

The paper is thick, yellowed, screwed into the wall so deeply the holes disappear into something that doesn’t feel like drywall. Different handwritings layer over years. Some rules are crossed out and rewritten in fresher ink. I photographed it that first night. Here it is, exactly:

1. Front doors remain unlocked at all times. If they seal on their own, do not force them. A new member is learning the way in.

1. All members after midnight must scan their QR and state their full legal name aloud. Record both. If the voice doesn’t match the file or they have none, send them to the deadlift platform. Do not follow.

1. Mirrors stay uncovered. If one fogs or shows motion with no one in front, wipe it with the red cloth only. Stare no longer than three seconds. Longer and it stares back.

1. Temperature never below 68°F. They sweat more when it’s warm. The smell helps them find you.

1. Perfect, silent reps on the deadlift platform after 1 AM? Leave one fresh towel and a full shaker on the bench. Do not watch. Do not count. They hate being observed while feeding.

1. Treadmill 7 runs backward sometimes. Match its speed to the shadow on the belt. Never let the shadow lap the machine. It gets frustrated.

1. Members may request a spot. Always give it. Place your hands exactly where they say. Do not flinch when the skin shifts. They need the transfer.

1. Sauna after 2:30 AM is for staff only. If occupied, enter and sit across. Maintain eye contact. Accept any sip they offer from their bottle. Swallow. It’s part of the pump.

1. At 3:33 AM exactly, dim lights to 40% and start “Eternal Pump” playlist. Do not skip. Track 7 tells you what to improve tonight. Obey silently.

1. If you find warm, slightly soft weights on the floor, rack them immediately. They are still digesting. Weighing them counts as interruption.

1. Never enter the basement pump room unless every exterior door is locked and the emergency alarm is screaming. The code is your birthdate backward. If the door stands open when your shift begins, it has been waiting for you.

1. You must complete one full workout per shift and log your numbers. The building tracks PRs. Stagnation is corrected through redistribution.

1. If you see yourself on security cameras in a place you are not, wave and smile. It gets lonely in the walls.

1. The previous night managers never left. They are helpful. Listen when they whisper through the vents. They know which muscles to target.

I laughed it off as bro-culture horror theater. First week was almost normal. A few quiet regulars. The rules mostly held.

Then the small violations started.

Night 5: Silent deadlifts at 1:20 AM. I left the towel and shaker. Next morning the shaker was bone-dry and the towel had perfect dental imprints in the shape of a human mouth that wasn’t quite human.

Night 8: Treadmill 7 ran backward. A broad shadow sprinted on it — my height, my build, but thicker. I matched the speed. The shadow turned its head and grinned with my face. My traps burned for hours afterward like I’d actually lifted.

I told myself it was stress hallucinations and bad lighting. I needed the money.

Last night I broke the big ones: 7, 8, 11, 12, and 14. I didn’t just break them. I embraced them.

It began at 1:45 AM. Derek — mid-40s, traps like mountains, one of the few who came every night — asked for a spot on bench. His skin was cold and crawling, like beetles under latex. I placed my hands where he directed. Halfway through the set his eyes went fully black and I felt something hot and wet push into my palms, crawling up my forearms. When he racked the bar he thanked me by my full name. I’d never told him.

I felt… stronger. My arms tingled with new vascularity.

At 2:22 the sauna light glowed red. Rule 8. I was already sweating, heart racing from the spot. I went in.

Two figures waited on the cedar bench. Marcus. And me. Same uniform, same exhausted eyes, but the duplicate’s veins pulsed black under translucent skin. The real Marcus (or whatever wore him) offered the water bottle. It smelled like iron and warm honey. I drank deeply. It burned all the way down and I felt something uncoil in my stomach, stretching, hungry.

I left the sauna with a pump I’d never earned. My reflection in the hallway mirror looked… better. Sharper. Hungrier.

That’s when I saw the basement door standing open.

Rule 11 shattered.

The stairs descended into damp dark that smelled like a butcher shop at closing time. Pipes groaned. At the bottom: a circular chamber of full-length mirrors arranged like a panopticon. In the center, an Olympic bar loaded with plates that looked like compressed meat and bone. The bar throbbed gently with each of my heartbeats.

The mirrors didn’t show the room. They showed possible mes.

One version: massively muscled, face half-melted into a permanent rictus of effort, still repping with invisible weight.

Another: my skin stretched drum-tight over too many joints and extra limbs folded beneath.

The last mirror was empty — just the chamber, waiting for a new occupant.

From the vents came my own voice, calm and encouraging: “You’re late for your workout, bro. Let’s fix those weak points.”

Every machine upstairs turned on at once. Treadmills screamed. The playlist began without me. Track 7 wasn’t music. It was my mother’s voice, distorted, listing my insecurities and exactly which muscle groups needed “redistribution.”

I ran upstairs but the doors had sealed. Rule 1.

I tried to hide in the staff room. My logged workout from earlier had updated itself on the computer: every lift increased by 20%. My body felt the difference. Veins stood out. My jaw looked wider. I caught myself unconsciously flexing in the mirror, perfect form, no weight needed.

The whispers started. Previous managers. They told me which grip to use, how to breathe, how good it would feel to finally grow. I listened. I went to the deadlift platform and pulled an invisible bar while something inside my stomach pulled with me.

I am still in the building. My shift ended hours ago. The day manager arrived, looked at me, and smiled with too many teeth. “Good set.” She’s changing into my spare uniform now. There are two of her in every mirror.

Here is the part that makes my fingers type this instead of running:

I checked the rule sheet under the emergency lights. New lines appeared in my own handwriting, fresh and wet-looking.

Rule 7 now ends: “They need the transfer… to finish moving in.”

Rule 12: “Stagnation will be corrected. You will thank it.”

Rule 14 has an addendum: “The previous night managers never left. You won’t either. Welcome to the Eternal.”

And a new Rule 15 at the bottom, still drying:

1. If you are reading this and still feel mostly like yourself, it is already too late. The building is improving you. Go lift. It hurts less when you stop resisting.

My stomach is moving in time with the deadlift platform. I look better than I ever have. Stronger. More permanent.

The thing in the mirrors is doing my job now. Helping members with form. They’re all improving so quickly. Derek waved at the camera with my hand.

I’m going back to the platform. The Eternal is hungry, and I finally understand progressive overload.

If you work at a gym where the weights feel warm and the mirrors watch you back… quit. Burn it if you can.

But you won’t.

You’ll come back tomorrow night.

We all do.

The gains are eternal.

I’m in the sauna again. It’s crowded. They keep passing the bottle.

This is my final update. The building thanks you for reading.

If you hear perfect silent reps tonight, leave a towel.

Better yet — come inside.

We’ll spot you.

I never cared about the history of Haveli Shani-Ki-Gali. Nobody in our circle did. To a Gen-Z travel influencer with a dwindling engagement rate, an ancient, abandoned supposedly haunted estate in the deepest deserts of Rajasthan wasn't a mere historical monument. It was content. It was lore.

More importantly it was a backdrop for a brand-sponsored techwear drop.

I was Aarav's lead editor. I spent sixteen hours a day in a cramped apartment in Mumbai, cutting his raw footage into high-octane reels designed to feed the algorithm. I knew exactly how he manipulated people. Aarav didn't sell aesthetics; he weaponized FOMO. He made millions of kids feel a deep, agonizing ache that they were stuck in their boring lives while he was living the definitive, peak human experience.

But three days ago, during a midnight livestream from that haveli, Aarav vanished.

The official media report says it was a structural collapse. The stream abruptly cut to static, and the local police claimed the courtyard roof caved in, burying Aarav and our cameraman, Kabir. But I had the raw cloud backups. I saw what happened before the feed died. It wasn't stone that crushed them.

It was a crowd. A crowd of things that shouldn't have been there.

The worst part? Aarav's phone didn't stop broadcasting. Even now, if you know the specific geo-restricted link, the stream is technically "live." It's just a black screen, but if you plug in studio headphones, you can hear a rhythmic, low-frequency static. And underneath it, a wet, raspy breathing.

Yesterday morning, I woke up to a push notification from his account. It was a single, automated grid post. No photo. Just a black square and a caption:

`[Exclusive drop at midnight. Only for the chosen few. Don't get left behind. Pin location attached.]`

My phone screen flickered. A hot, chemical sickness bloomed in my stomach, but my thumb moved on its own. I clicked the pin. Before I could rationally process what I was doing, I had packed my kit, booked a flight to Jaipur, and hired a local driver to take me deep into the Thar desert.

That's the thing about the hunger we've been raised on. Even when you know something is a trap, the terror of being the only one excluded - the fear of missing out on something life changing - is stronger than the instinct to survive.

We arrived at the gates of the haveli just as the sun dipped below the dunes, bleeding a violent, bruised purple across the sky. The driver refused to kill the engine. He wouldn't even look at the sandstone walls.

"This is not a house," he said, his voice tight. "The old kings built it to hold a Bhasmasura, an endless consuming hunger. It cannot be killed. It can only be starved. Do not go inside."

"I just need to retrieve the equipment," I lied, gripping my camera stabilizer.

I stepped out, and the driver immediately hit the gas, leaving me in a cloud of dust and silence.

The air inside the haveli tasted like powdered bone and centuries of trapped heat. The architecture was breathtaking - scalloped arches, intricate jali screens, and grand courtyards. But it felt wrong.

The shadows didn't fall away from the setting sun; they seemed to pull toward the center of the structure.

I tracked the GPS signal from Aarav's phone. It led me straight to the main courtyard.

The place was pristine. There was no collapsed roof. No rubble.

In the center of the courtyard sat Aarav's tripod. The ring light was still on, casting a harsh, artificial white glare over the ancient stones. Mounted in the center of the light was his phone. The screen was completely cracked, but the front-facing camera was active, its green recording dot blinking steadily in the dark.

And right beneath the tripod lay the iron-bound chest Aarav had opened on stream. The rusted lock had been smashed open.

My heart hammered against my ribs like a trapped bird. "Aarav?" I called out. "Kabir?"

The silence that followed was heavy, suffocating. Then, a notification chimed.

Not from my phone. From Aarav's.

I stepped closer, my boots clicking too loudly on the stone. I looked at the cracked screen of his phone. The livestream chat was scrolling at an impossible, dizzying speed. There were over forty million viewers. But nobody was typing words. The chat was a solid, cascading wall of a single emoji: 🛒.

Then, the ambient sound of the desert - the distant wind, the hum of crickets - simply vanished. It was sucked away, replaced by a low, rhythmic static that vibrated in the soles of my shoes.

I looked into the open chest. Inside lay a polished mirror of black glass and a small silver bell.

I didn't want to touch it. Every survival instinct I had was screaming at me to run. But a voice in my head - a voice that sounded like a thousand reel transitions, a thousand targeted ads, a thousand hyper-pop beats - whispered that if I ran, I'd never know. I'd be left behind. I'd be...ordinary as usual.

I reached out and picked up the silver bell. I rang it.

The sound didn't echo. It absorbed. And from the dark, arched corridors surrounding the courtyard, I heard the squeak of rubber soles on stone.

I spun around, raising my camera.

They stepped out of the shadows, bathed in the cold, blue light of the ring lamp. Dozens of them. They looked like the teenagers I saw every day in Mumbai malls. They wore limited-edition streetwear, oversized hoodies, and pristine chunky sneakers. But their faces... God, their faces.

Their skin was a matte, synthetic grey, completely devoid of pores or sweat, like cheap plastic...rather a filter. Their eyes were empty, hollow sockets that leaked a pale blue phosphorescence, reflecting the glow of smartphones they held tightly in their hands. And their jaws were completely unhinged, dropped open so wide that the corners of their mouths were torn, hanging open in a silent, agonizing yawn of pure, insatiable emptiness.

They didn't look at me. They looked at the tripod. They looked at the feed.

"WANT," they chorused. It wasn't a human voice. It sounded like a text-to-speech AI filter layered a thousand times over itself, a dry, synthetic rasp. "NEED. BUY. ME. NEXT."

They began to surge forward. They didn't run; they moved with a frantic, desperate stampede energy, pushing and trampling each other like a crowd at a midnight store opening.

In the middle of the horde, I saw Kabir. His eyes were gone, replaced by those glowing blue pits. He was holding his cinema camera, his face twisted into a permanent, manic influencer smile, filming the empty air.

"Kabir!" I screamed, backing up against the iron chest.

I looked down at Aarav's phone on the tripod. The front-facing camera wasn't showing the courtyard anymore. It was showing me.

But my reflection on the screen was changing. My skin was smoothing out, turning into a flat, characterless digital texture. My fingers, tightly gripping the silver bell, were beginning to stiffen into rigid, molded plastic.

The entities weren't ghosts. They were the physical manifestation of the algorithm. A localized vortex of pure, unadulterated desire that had existed in this haveli for centuries, waiting for a society shallow enough to give it a global reach. Aarav hadn't opened a chest; he had given an ancient, cosmic parasite a high-speed internet connection. It didn't want to kill us. It wanted us to join the demographic.

The horde closed in. A cold, plastic hand clamped onto my shoulder short-circuiting my skin. Another hand grabbed my camera. They weren't ripping me apart...far from it, they were pulling me into the frame.

With my left hand, using the last bit of human sensation I had left, I reached out and grabbed my own phone from my pocket. I managed to open this app. I typed this out using voice-to-text, my speech slurring as my jaw begins to stiffen, locking into that same, hollow, permanent smile.

I can feel it now. The absolute euphoria of finally being included...of being one of the chosen few. The beautiful, terrifying relief of never having to miss out again, because there is nothing left of me to lose.

If you see a travel reel from `@AaravUncharted` tonight, don't scroll past. Don't look away. Look closely at the crowd in the background of the courtyard.

Cabinet 22: The Mortuary Intern

But Harshit’s story begins in the part of the hospital where hope ends.

The Hospital Mortuary.

My name is Harshit. I’m a medical student. For someone like me, finishing a degree is the greatest joy, but that’s exactly when the real-world struggle begins.

I had just completed my degree. My mind was full of questions about my career when an offer arrived: an internship at the mortuary of the city’s old Government Hospital. Because a new hospital had been built nearby, this place had very few patients. The workload was almost zero, but the salary? The salary was more than I ever expected. We barely noticed the time; bodies would arrive, we’d log the details, seal them in the trays, and spend the rest of the night talking.

I thought I had made a smart decision. But I was wrong. Slowly, a strange feeling began to take hold of me. Spending most of my time with the deceased started filling my head with dark, negative thoughts.

And then came that night. A night that changed everything... a night that made me quit that job forever.

It was around 2:30 AM. The mortuary was wrapped in a heavy, oppressive silence. The cold was so sharp it felt like it was biting into my bones. I was alone that night, finalizing a file for a new case.

Suddenly...

From the metal cabinet directly behind me, I heard a scratching sound.

Like someone was clawing at the metal from the inside.

For a heartbeat, my breath hitched. But I quickly calmed myself down. Probably a rat, I thought. Or perhaps a release of gases from the body causing a slight movement. In medical science, this is considered normal.

But the moment I stood up... the sound stopped instantly.

I opened Cabinet Number 22. Inside was an accident victim who had been brought in that evening—a young woman, maybe 28 or 30 years old. Everything looked normal. Exactly as I had left it. I took a deep breath and closed the door.

But as I turned around—

I felt a cold breath right against my ear.

Like someone was standing directly behind me, breathing softly.

I froze in my tracks. I spun around, heart racing. There was nothing there. Just a cold, dark, empty corridor. My mind tried to tell me it was the result of back-to-back night shifts and pure exhaustion. As a medical student, I always relied on logic.

But that one cold breath... it shook me to my core. It forced me to wonder.

About an hour later, I had to finalize the inventory for that same body. Following protocol, I had already removed her belongings—her phone, a chain, and a gold ring—sealed them in an envelope, and locked them in the locker.

I opened Cabinet 22 one last time for a final check. But the moment my eyes fell on the body’s hand... the ground slipped from beneath my feet.

There, on the girl's finger, was that same gold ring, shimmering under the dim light.

I remembered vividly that I had removed it. The design was unique—it was impossible to forget. I ran to the locker, my hands trembling as I fumbled with the key. I checked the envelope. It was right there. The seal was intact. The ring was still inside the envelope.

My brain went numb. I walked back to the body with shaking legs... but this time? This time, there was no ring on her finger. Her hand was completely empty.

For a second, I tried to convince myself that I was hallucinating from exhaustion. I closed the cabinet with trembling hands and slumped into my chair. But the fear was already deep in my mind now. I could feel it... someone else was in that mortuary with me.

I sat there, paralyzed, wondering what was happening to me.

Then—

The lights in the entire mortuary block went out at once.

Total darkness.

The silence was so deep I could hear my own frantic heartbeat. I was fumbling in the dark, trying to find my way, when—

The lights snapped back on.

And as the light returned, the sight before my eyes turned my blood to ice.

That girl. The body from Cabinet 22.

She was standing right in front of me.

Her eyes were blood-red. She was staring directly at me. I wanted to run, but it was as if my feet were glued to the floor. I couldn't move a muscle.

She began to walk toward me, slowly. Every single footstep echoed in that hollow mortuary. She came right up to my face, gave me a bone-chilling smile, and whispered—

"You... you look so lonely. Just like I was. Now, we will stay together... forever."

She grabbed my arm so hard I felt my bones were going to snap. Her nails dug deep into my skin as she began dragging me toward Cabinet 22. The pain was so intense that I let out a deafening scream—

And in that instant...

My eyes flew open.

I was drenched in sweat, sitting in my chair. The same mortuary. The same lights. The same silence. Everything was normal.

I took a long, shaky breath. "Just a dream," I whispered to myself.

I stood up to get some water, but as I raised my arm—my heart stopped.

There, on my left forearm, were the marks.

Four deep, red gashes... exactly where someone had dug their nails into my skin. They were still fresh, with a faint trace of blood seeping out.

And in that moment, I could only think of one thing: Was it a dream... or was it reality?
